topics.name: Stamen
topics.kicker: Male part of a flower · An anther on a stalk called a filament
topics.briefing: A stamen is the male part of a flower: a slender stalk called a filament, topped by an anther that makes pollen. When a bee brushes past, the anthers dust its hairy body with pollen, which it carries to the sticky stigma of the next flower it visits. In the 1700s, the botanist Carl Linnaeus sorted plants into groups mostly by counting their stamens.
topics.answerHtml: Stamen (accept stamens or stamina; prompt on androecium or male part; do not accept “anther,” “filament,” or “pistil”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Carl Linnaeus’s “sexual system” sorted plants into 24 classes based mainly on the number of these structures in each flower, with names such as Monandria for plants that have only one. His orders within those classes were based on counting pistils.
tossups.r: Each of these structures has a pollen-making anther. For 10 points, name these male parts of a flower.

tossups.p: In the ABC model of plant development, B-class and C-class genes working together make these structures form in the third whorl of a flower. Agamous [“AG-uh-mus”] mutants of Arabidopsis [“uh-RAB-ih-DOP-sis”] grow petals in place of these structures.
tossups.r: Each of these structures is made of a filament topped by an anther. For 10 points, name these male reproductive organs of flowers.

tossups.p: In hibiscus, hollyhocks, and other mallows, these structures are fused into a single tube that surrounds the style. Pea flowers usually have ten of them, with nine joined together and one left free.
tossups.r: Together they make up the androecium, and each one ends in a pollen-making anther. For 10 points, name these male parts of a flower.

tossups.p: Plants in the mint family usually have four of these structures, two long and two short, while plants in the mustard family usually have six, four long and two short. Lilies and many other monocots usually have six of them, arranged in two rings of three.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these male organs of a flower, each of which holds up an anther on a filament.

tossups.p: Touching the base of these structures in a barberry makes them snap inward toward the center of the flower, dusting the visiting insect. In mountain laurel, these structures are bent back into little pockets in the petals and spring up to fling pollen when a bee lands.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these male parts of a flower, each made of an anther and a filament.

tossups.p: A nourishing layer of cells called the tapetum [“tuh-PEE-tum”] feeds the young pollen developing inside these structures. When the pollen is ripe, the pollen sacs at the top of each of these structures split open, a process called dehiscence [“dih-HISS-ens”].
tossups.r: Those sacs sit in the anther. For 10 points, name these male flower parts, whose thin stalks are called filaments.

tossups.p: Blueberry versions of these structures release pollen only through tiny holes at their tips, so bumblebees shake the pollen loose by rapidly vibrating their flight muscles, a behavior called sonication or buzz pollination. Honey bees do not perform this trick.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these pollen-making male parts of a flower, each topped with an anther.

tossups.p: Florists often snip the pollen-covered tips off these structures in lilies so their pollen will not stain petals or clothing. Plant breeders, including Gregor Mendel with his peas, remove these structures from a flower before they ripen so the flower cannot pollinate itself.
tossups.r: Their pollen must reach a pistil to make seeds. For 10 points, name these male flower parts, each tipped with an anther.

tossups.p: Many double-petaled roses and camellias get their extra petals when some of these structures develop as petals instead. Sterile versions of these structures, which make no pollen, can look like small scales or petals.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these male reproductive structures of flowers, which usually make pollen in anthers on top of filaments.

tossups.p: Inside these structures, cells called microsporocytes [“my-kroh-SPOR-uh-sytes”] undergo meiosis, and each one makes four microspores. Each microspore then divides by mitosis to form a pollen grain with a tube cell and a generative cell.
tossups.r: This all happens in the anther at the tip of each of these structures. For 10 points, name these male parts of a flower.

tossups.p: In corn, the small flowers in the tassel have only these structures, while the flowers on the ear have only pistils, whose long styles form the silks. A flower that has both these structures and pistils is called “perfect.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these male parts of flowers, each made of an anther and a filament.

tossups.p: Grasses and other wind-pollinated plants often have long, dangling versions of these structures that hang outside their small, plain flowers, so the breeze can shake pollen out of them. Ragweed plants release huge clouds of pollen from these structures in late summer.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these male parts of a flower, each made of an anther on a filament.

tossups.p: The name of these structures comes from the Latin word for a thread on a loom. All of them in a single flower make up a whorl whose name means “man’s house” in Greek, the androecium [“an-DREE-see-um”].
tossups.r: They usually stand in a ring around the pistil. For 10 points, name these male flower parts that make pollen in their anthers.

tossups.p: In most orchids, a single one of these structures is fused with the style and stigma into a part called the column, and its pollen is packed into sticky bundles called pollinia [“puh-LIN-ee-uh”] that cling to visiting insects.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these male parts of a flower, each made of an anther on a filament.

tossups.p: The red “bristles” of bottlebrush plants and the fluffy pink puffs of the silk tree are made mostly of these structures, which in those plants are unusually long and brightly colored. Each one is tipped with a tiny, pollen-filled knob.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these male flower parts, each made of an anther on top of a filament.

trap.title: Whole stamen or anther?
trap.body: The anther is only the pollen-making tip of this structure, and the filament is only its stalk, so neither one earns credit when the question asks for the whole male organ. The pistil, or carpel, is the female part, and Pollen and Flowers are separate answer lines. All the stamens of one flower together are called the androecium, which only earns a prompt.
trap.fix: “This pollen-making sac” or “this tip” wants anther, and “this thin stalk” wants filament. “These male structures,” or anything built from both an anther and a filament, means stamen. Say “stamens” when the question says “these.”
trap.line: Real answer line: Stamen (accept stamens or stamina; prompt on androecium or male part; do not accept “anther,” “filament,” or “pistil”)

topics.name: Glycolysis
topics.kicker: First stage of cellular respiration · Splits glucose into two pyruvates
topics.dates: All ten steps worked out by 1940
topics.briefing: Glycolysis is the first step cells take to get energy out of sugar. In ten enzyme-run steps in the cytoplasm, it splits one six-carbon glucose molecule into two three-carbon pyruvate molecules, for a net gain of two ATP. It does not need oxygen, so nearly every living thing can do it, from bacteria to the muscle cells powering a hard sprint.
topics.answerHtml: Glycolysis (accept Embden–Meyerhof–Parnas pathway or EMP pathway; prompt on cellular respiration; do not accept “gluconeogenesis” or “fermentation”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Phosphofructokinase [“FOSS-foh-FROOK-toh-KY-nayss”] catalyzes the committed step of this pathway, and it is slowed down by high levels of ATP and citrate but sped up by AMP. Another enzyme in this pathway, aldolase, splits a six-carbon sugar into two three-carbon pieces.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this first stage of cellular respiration, which breaks glucose into two molecules of pyruvate.

tossups.p: Otto Warburg noticed that cancer cells rely heavily on this pathway even when plenty of oxygen is available, a pattern called the Warburg effect. Mature red blood cells, which have no mitochondria, make all of their ATP through this pathway.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this ten-step pathway in the cytoplasm that splits glucose into pyruvate.

tossups.p: Arthur Harden and William Young found that adding phosphate made yeast juice ferment sugar faster, and they identified a sugar with two phosphate groups that builds up during this pathway. Earlier, Eduard Buchner had shown that juice from ground-up yeast cells could still ferment sugar.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this anaerobic pathway that turns one glucose into two pyruvate molecules and nets two ATP.

tossups.p: Otto Meyerhof, who shared a 1922 Nobel Prize for studying how working muscles make lactic acid, is one of three scientists, along with Gustav Embden and Jakub Parnas, whose names are sometimes given to this pathway. All ten of its steps had been worked out by 1940.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this pathway that splits glucose into two pyruvate molecules in the cytoplasm.

tossups.p: Triose phosphate isomerase, an enzyme in this pathway, is often called a “perfect” enzyme because it works about as fast as its target molecules can reach it. In the next step, glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate dehydrogenase adds a phosphate group and passes electrons to NAD+, making NADH.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this first stage of cellular respiration, which happens in the cytoplasm.

tossups.p: Fluoride blocks enolase, the enzyme that makes phosphoenolpyruvate in this pathway, so blood samples for sugar tests are often collected in tubes containing sodium fluoride, which stops blood cells from using up the sugar. The enzyme pyruvate kinase then makes ATP in the final step.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this ten-step pathway that nets two ATP from each glucose molecule.

tossups.p: In the first step of this pathway, hexokinase spends an ATP to attach a phosphate group to a sugar, trapping the sugar inside the cell. Liver cells use a related enzyme, glucokinase, which only works quickly when sugar levels are high.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this pathway that splits glucose into two pyruvate molecules without needing oxygen.

tossups.p: This pathway’s first half is called the energy-investment phase because it uses up two ATP, while its second half, the payoff phase, makes four ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation. That payoff phase also produces two molecules of NADH.
tossups.r: That leaves a net gain of two ATP. For 10 points, name this first stage of cellular respiration.

tossups.p: When oxygen runs short, cells regenerate the NAD+ that this pathway needs through fermentation, turning its end product into lactic acid in muscle cells or into ethanol and carbon dioxide in yeast. That lets this pathway keep making small amounts of ATP.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this pathway in the cytoplasm that breaks glucose into pyruvate.

tossups.p: Gluconeogenesis builds new glucose in the liver by running roughly in reverse of this pathway, using different enzymes to get around its three one-way steps. In the Cori cycle, lactic acid made in working muscles after this pathway travels to the liver to be rebuilt into glucose.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this first stage of cellular respiration, which turns glucose into pyruvate and nets two ATP.

tossups.p: In the Pasteur effect, yeast cells break down sugar through this pathway much more slowly when oxygen is present, since aerobic respiration gets far more ATP from each sugar molecule. This pathway is so ancient that nearly every living thing, from bacteria to people, uses it.
tossups.r: It does not need oxygen. For 10 points, name this pathway that splits glucose into two three-carbon pyruvate molecules.

tossups.p: The fourth step of this pathway splits fructose 1,6-bisphosphate into two three-carbon sugars, dihydroxyacetone [“dy-hy-DROK-see-ASS-uh-tohn”] phosphate and glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate, which an isomerase then interconverts. This pathway’s name comes from Greek words meaning “sweet” and “splitting.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this first stage of cellular respiration, which breaks one glucose into two pyruvate molecules in the cytoplasm.

tossups.p: When oxygen is plentiful, the end products of this pathway are carried into mitochondria, where an enzyme complex turns each one into acetyl-CoA [“uh-SEE-tul koh-AY”] and carbon dioxide to feed the Krebs cycle. Unlike those later stages, this pathway takes place in the cytoplasm.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this first stage of cellular respiration, which splits glucose into pyruvate.

tossups.p: The signaling molecule fructose 2,6-bisphosphate strongly speeds up this pathway by switching on phosphofructokinase. During a hard sprint, muscle cells lean heavily on this pathway, which makes ATP quickly without oxygen but releases only a small share of the energy stored in sugar.
tossups.r: Each glucose gives a net of two ATP this way. For 10 points, name this first stage of cellular respiration.

tossups.p: In this pathway, phosphoglycerate kinase moves a phosphate group from 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate onto ADP, making the first ATP of the payoff phase. A mutase then shifts the remaining phosphate group to a different carbon atom. Both steps happen twice for every glucose molecule, since that sugar was split in half earlier.
tossups.r: It nets two ATP and two NADH. For 10 points, name this ten-step pathway that turns glucose into pyruvate.

clues.t: The first stage of cellular respiration
Splits one glucose (six carbons) into two pyruvate molecules (three carbons each)
Nets two ATP (it makes four and spends two) and two NADH for each glucose
Takes place in the cytoplasm, not in the mitochondria
Does not need oxygen (it is anaerobic), so nearly every living thing can do it
Ten steps, each run by its own enzyme
An energy-investment phase spends two ATP; a payoff phase then makes four
Hexokinase attaches a phosphate to glucose in the first step, trapping it inside the cell
Phosphofructokinase runs the committed step; ATP and citrate slow it down, and AMP speeds it up
Fermentation regenerates NAD+ so it can keep going without oxygen: lactic acid in muscles, ethanol and carbon dioxide in yeast
Makes ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation, at the phosphoglycerate kinase and pyruvate kinase steps
With oxygen, its pyruvate enters the mitochondria and becomes acetyl-CoA for the Krebs cycle
Mature red blood cells, which lack mitochondria, make all of their ATP this way
Muscle cells lean on it during a hard sprint because it makes ATP quickly without oxygen
Its name comes from Greek words meaning “sweet” and “splitting”
The Warburg effect: cancer cells rely heavily on it even when plenty of oxygen is around
Arthur Harden and William Young found that phosphate sped up fermentation in yeast juice and identified a sugar with two phosphate groups
Eduard Buchner showed that juice from ground-up yeast cells could still ferment sugar (1907 Nobel Prize)
Also named for Gustav Embden, Otto Meyerhof, and Jakub Parnas; Meyerhof shared a 1922 Nobel Prize for work on lactic acid in muscles
Triose phosphate isomerase is called a “perfect” enzyme: it works about as fast as its target molecules can reach it
Glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate dehydrogenase adds a phosphate group and makes NADH
Aldolase splits fructose 1,6-bisphosphate into two three-carbon sugars, DHAP and glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate
Fluoride blocks enolase, the enzyme that makes phosphoenolpyruvate, so blood-sugar samples go in sodium fluoride tubes
Liver cells use glucokinase, which works quickly only when sugar levels are high
Gluconeogenesis runs roughly in reverse, bypassing its three one-way steps; the Cori cycle sends muscle lactic acid to the liver to become glucose
The Pasteur effect: yeast run it much more slowly when oxygen is present
Fructose 2,6-bisphosphate speeds it up by switching on phosphofructokinase

trap.title: Not its reverse
trap.body: Gluconeogenesis runs this pathway roughly backward to build new glucose, and glycogenolysis breaks stored glycogen down into glucose, so the long sugar-names can blur together. Fermentation is a separate step that follows this pathway when oxygen is missing, and the Krebs cycle follows it when oxygen is present.
trap.fix: Splitting glucose into two pyruvates in the cytoplasm, hexokinase, phosphofructokinase, aldolase, or a net of two ATP all mean glycolysis. Making new glucose means gluconeogenesis, breaking down glycogen means glycogenolysis, and turning pyruvate into lactic acid or ethanol means fermentation.
trap.line: Real answer line: Glycolysis (accept Embden–Meyerhof–Parnas pathway or EMP pathway; prompt on cellular respiration; do not accept “gluconeogenesis” or “fermentation”)

topics.name: Thylakoids
topics.kicker: Coin-shaped sacs inside chloroplasts · Where the light reactions happen
topics.briefing: Thylakoids are flattened, coin-shaped sacs inside chloroplasts, stacked into piles called grana like pancakes. Their membranes are packed with chlorophyll and the rest of the machinery for the light reactions: they capture sunlight, split water to release oxygen, and pump hydrogen ions into their hollow centers to power ATP synthase. The sugar-building Calvin cycle then runs in the fluid around them, the stroma.
topics.answerHtml: Thylakoids (accept thylakoid membranes; prompt on grana or granum; do not accept “stroma,” “lumen,” or “chloroplasts”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In a famous 1966 “acid bath” experiment, André Jagendorf and Ernest Uribe soaked these structures in an acidic solution and then moved them into a basic one with ADP and phosphate, and they made ATP in total darkness. That result strongly supported Peter Mitchell’s theory of chemiosmosis.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these coin-shaped sacs inside chloroplasts, stacked into grana, where the light reactions occur.

tossups.p: A cluster of four manganese atoms and one calcium atom in these structures splits water molecules, releasing oxygen gas and sending hydrogen ions into their inner space. That oxygen-evolving complex is part of photosystem II, which sits in their membranes.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these flattened sacs inside chloroplasts where the light-dependent reactions of photosynthesis happen.

tossups.p: Plastocyanin [“plass-toh-SY-uh-nin”], a small protein containing copper, carries electrons through the fluid inside these structures, while plastoquinone [“plass-toh-KWIN-ohn”] shuttles electrons within their membranes. Both carriers help pass electrons from photosystem II to photosystem I, and ferredoxin then carries electrons away from photosystem I on the outer side.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these membrane sacs inside chloroplasts, stacked into grana, where sunlight is captured.

tossups.p: The knob-shaped part of each ATP synthase in these structures’ membranes faces outward, so ATP is released into the surrounding stroma. In bright light, the inside of these structures becomes far more acidic than the stroma as hydrogen ions pile up there.
tossups.r: That inner space is the lumen. For 10 points, name these stacked sacs inside chloroplasts.

tossups.p: Photosystem II gathers mostly in the tightly stacked regions of these structures, while photosystem I and ATP synthase sit mostly in the unstacked regions, where they can reach the stroma. The unstacked parts that link one stack to the next are called stroma lamellae [“luh-MEL-ee”].
tossups.r: The stacks are called grana. For 10 points, name these flattened sacs inside chloroplasts.

tossups.p: Photosystem I and photosystem II, two protein complexes in the membranes of these structures, are numbered in the order they were discovered, even though electrons pass through photosystem II first. Each photosystem has an antenna of pigment molecules that funnels light energy to a reaction center.
tossups.r: Their membranes hold chlorophyll and capture light. For 10 points, name these sacs inside chloroplasts.

tossups.p: Lynn Margulis championed the idea that chloroplasts inherited these structures from cyanobacteria that were swallowed by an ancient cell and never digested. Cyanobacteria still have these structures right in their cytoplasm, since they have no chloroplasts.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these membrane sacs, stacked into grana in plants, where the light reactions take place.

tossups.p: Seedlings grown in total darkness form a lattice of tubes called a prolamellar [“proh-luh-MEL-er”] body instead of these structures. Once light arrives, that lattice reorganizes into these structures as chlorophyll is made, turning pale etioplasts into green chloroplasts.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these coin-shaped sacs, stacked into grana, where chloroplasts capture light energy.

tossups.p: In 1941, Samuel Ruben and Martin Kamen used water labeled with the heavy isotope oxygen-18 to show that the oxygen plants release comes from water, which is split in these structures. That splitting, called photolysis, also supplies the electrons that flow through their membranes.
tossups.r: They are stacked into grana. For 10 points, name these sacs inside chloroplasts where the light reactions occur.

tossups.p: In 1937, Robin Hill showed that isolated chloroplasts could release oxygen in light if given a chemical that accepts electrons. In classroom versions of that Hill reaction, the blue dye DCPIP turns colorless as it picks up electrons from these structures.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these stacked sacs where the light-dependent reactions of photosynthesis take place.

tossups.p: In 1954, Daniel Arnon showed that chloroplasts can make ATP using light, a process called photophosphorylation that happens on these structures. In cyclic electron flow, electrons from photosystem I loop back through these structures’ membranes, making extra ATP but no NADPH.
tossups.r: These sacs are stacked into grana inside chloroplasts. For 10 points, name these structures where the light reactions happen.

tossups.p: The weed killers DCMU and atrazine block the flow of electrons out of photosystem II, which is embedded in the membranes of these structures. Without that electron flow, a plant cannot make the ATP and NADPH its Calvin cycle needs.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these coin-shaped sacs inside chloroplasts where the light reactions happen.

tossups.p: The name of these structures comes from a Greek word for a sack or pouch. The fluid-filled space inside each one is called the lumen, and the membrane around it is packed with chlorophyll and other pigments.
tossups.r: Stacks of them, called grana, look like piles of coins inside chloroplasts. For 10 points, name these sacs.

tossups.p: The cytochrome b6f complex in these structures’ membranes pumps extra hydrogen ions inward as electrons pass through it. Electrons in these structures follow a zigzag path called the Z-scheme, from the reaction center P680 in photosystem II to P700 in photosystem I.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these stacked sacs inside chloroplasts where light energy is captured.

tossups.p: These structures are often compared to the cristae of mitochondria, since both are membranes that hold an electron transport chain and use a flow of hydrogen ions through ATP synthase to make ATP. Light-harvesting complexes in their membranes hold chlorophylls and orange carotenoids.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these sacs, stacked into grana, where the light reactions of photosynthesis happen.

trap.title: Sac, stack, or space?
trap.body: Thylakoids are the individual membrane sacs. A stack of them is a granum (plural grana), which earns only a prompt; the fluid around them is the stroma; and the space inside each one is the lumen. The chloroplast is the whole organelle, so none of those answers is the same as this one.
trap.fix: “These sacs” or “these membranes” where the light reactions happen means thylakoids. “These stacks” means grana, “this fluid” where the Calvin cycle runs means stroma, and “this inner space” where hydrogen ions pile up means lumen.
trap.line: Real answer line: Thylakoids (accept thylakoid membranes; prompt on grana or granum; do not accept “stroma,” “lumen,” or “chloroplasts”)

topics.name: Uracil
topics.kicker: RNA base that pairs with adenine · Takes thymine’s place in RNA
topics.dates: Found in the RNA of every living cell
topics.briefing: Uracil is one of the four chemical letters, or bases, in RNA, abbreviated U. It takes the place of thymine, the base DNA uses, so when a gene is copied into messenger RNA, every adenine in the DNA gets matched with uracil instead of thymine. The two bases are near twins: thymine is simply uracil with one extra methyl group attached.
topics.answerHtml: Uracil (accept U; prompt on uridine or pyrimidine; do not accept “thymine”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1961, Marshall Nirenberg and Heinrich Matthaei added a synthetic RNA made of nothing but this base to a cell-free system and got a protein chain made only of phenylalanine, cracking the first word of the genetic code.
tossups.r: In RNA, it pairs with adenine. For 10 points, name this base that takes the place of thymine in RNA.

tossups.p: When cytosine loses an amino group, it turns into this base, so cells use a repair enzyme found by Nobel laureate Tomas Lindahl to snip this base out of DNA. That is one reason DNA uses a methylated look-alike of this base instead.
tossups.r: That look-alike is thymine. For 10 points, name this RNA base that pairs with adenine.

tossups.p: Katalin Karikó [“KAH-tah-lin KAH-ree-koh”] and Drew Weissman shared the 2023 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for showing that messenger RNA made with a modified form of this base’s nucleoside does not set off a strong immune reaction, work that helped make mRNA vaccines against COVID-19 possible.
tossups.r: That modified nucleoside is pseudouridine. For 10 points, name this pyrimidine base found in RNA in place of thymine.

tossups.p: In 2023, scientists reported finding this base in samples that Japan’s Hayabusa2 spacecraft brought back from the asteroid Ryugu. It had earlier been detected in the Murchison meteorite, which fell in Australia in 1969.
tossups.r: In RNA, it pairs with adenine. For 10 points, name this base that replaces thymine in RNA.

tossups.p: Francis Crick’s 1966 wobble hypothesis explained how this base, at the first position of a transfer RNA’s anticodon, can pair with guanine as well as with its usual partner. That loose fit lets one transfer RNA read more than one codon.
tossups.r: Its usual partner is adenine. For 10 points, name this base that RNA uses instead of thymine.

tossups.p: All three stop codons in the standard genetic code begin with this base, and the usual start codon has it as its middle letter. All six codons for the amino acid leucine also have it in the middle.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this base, found in messenger RNA, that pairs with adenine.

tossups.p: The enzyme thymidylate synthase makes the thymine nucleotides that DNA needs by adding a methyl group to a nucleotide carrying this base. Like cytosine, this base is a pyrimidine, built on a single six-membered ring with two nitrogen atoms.
tossups.r: In RNA, it pairs with adenine. For 10 points, name this base that takes thymine’s place in RNA.

tossups.p: Before glucose can be added to a growing glycogen chain, it is first attached to a nucleotide carrying this base, forming an activated sugar. Plants use the same kind of activated sugar to build sucrose and cellulose.
tossups.r: Its nucleoside is uridine. For 10 points, name this pyrimidine base that pairs with adenine in RNA.

tossups.p: When cells build pyrimidine nucleotides from scratch, the first finished one carries this base, and the other pyrimidine nucleotides are made from it. For example, cells make cytosine nucleotides by adding an amino group to triphosphate nucleotides of this base.
tossups.r: It pairs with adenine. For 10 points, name this RNA base, which takes the place of thymine.

tossups.p: Replacing one hydrogen atom of this base with fluorine makes a common chemotherapy drug, which blocks the enzyme cells use to make the thymine nucleotides that DNA needs. Most DNA contains this base only by mistake or as a result of damage.
tossups.r: In RNA, it pairs with adenine. For 10 points, name this base that RNA uses in place of thymine.

tossups.p: The D arm of a transfer RNA molecule is named for a modified form of this base’s nucleoside that it often contains. This base forms just two hydrogen bonds with its partner, one fewer than guanine and cytosine share.
tossups.r: That modified nucleoside is dihydrouridine [“dy-HY-droh-YOOR-ih-deen”], and the partner is adenine. For 10 points, name this base that replaces thymine in RNA.

tossups.p: Viruses that store their genes as RNA, such as flu viruses and coronaviruses, carry this base in their genetic material instead of thymine. When a DNA template strand reading A-A-A is copied into messenger RNA, the resulting codon has this base in all three positions.
tossups.r: It pairs with adenine. For 10 points, name this pyrimidine base found in RNA but not normally in DNA.

tossups.p: Biologists who want to tag newly made RNA feed cells a radioactive nucleoside built from this base, while they tag newly made DNA with radioactive thymidine instead. Each RNA strand has this base wherever the DNA template it was copied from had an adenine.
tossups.r: Its nucleoside is uridine. For 10 points, name this base, found in RNA instead of thymine.

tossups.p: Har Gobind Khorana built RNA strands that alternated this base with cytosine, and they produced protein chains that alternated the amino acids serine and leucine. Khorana shared the 1968 Nobel Prize with Marshall Nirenberg and Robert Holley.
tossups.r: In RNA, it takes thymine’s place. For 10 points, name this base that pairs with adenine.

tossups.p: In 2025, scientists reported that samples NASA’s OSIRIS-REx spacecraft brought back from the asteroid Bennu contain all five bases found in DNA and RNA, including this one. This base’s chemical formula is C4H4N2O2.
tossups.r: Life normally uses it only in RNA, where it pairs with adenine. For 10 points, name this base.

Pairs with adenine, forming two hydrogen bonds
A pyrimidine, built on a single ring, like cytosine and thymine

Joined to the sugar ribose, it forms the nucleoside uridine
During transcription, RNA polymerase places it wherever the DNA template has an adenine

Tomas Lindahl found the repair enzyme that removes it from DNA; he shared the 2015 Nobel Prize in Chemistry
Karikó and Weissman (2023 Nobel) used pseudouridine in place of its nucleoside in mRNA, which helped make COVID-19 mRNA vaccines possible
Crick’s 1966 wobble hypothesis: at an anticodon’s first position it can pair with guanine as well as adenine
Thymidylate synthase adds a methyl group to a nucleotide of this base to make the thymine nucleotides DNA needs
